utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. The witness who is called to testify now requested the following protective measures, which has become traditional now: pseudonym and facial distortion. The motivation is the same reasons of securities. His testimony is supposed to go mostly to the following parts of our indictment: background, paragraph 7, 11; superior authority, paragraph 17, 14; general allegations, paragraphs from 18 through 21; count 1, paragraphs 26, 27, 30, 31, 34(a), (b), (d); counts 2 through 5, paragraph 35 through 38; count 21, paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Of course, while our witness is on the move, I would like the Trial Chamber for permission just maybe to lead in some irrelevant issues because our witness statement -- our prior -- our witness's prior statements are very comprehensive and some parts are quite irrelevant to our case but we cannot just throw them away from his story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have to remind you that we have to finish this witness today because this is the last day for this year. We could not afford to have a witness under oath for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. It's also for this very reason that I will skip some parts and maybe I will go through quickly through several parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How long do you expect that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I expect this witness to testify for about one hour and 30 minutes maybe. But this is maximum, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is going to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter] .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your request for protective measures has been granted by the Trial Chamber. Now you will have a pseudonym and you will be called Witness YY in this courtroom. You also will have face image distortion. In some parts of your testimony, perhaps we'll ask the Trial Chamber to go into private session. Now, you will be given a piece of paper with some name written on it. Please look at it and read it. If this is your name and the spelling is correct, date of birth is correct, just say "yes" without reading it aloud. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness YY, we'll go straight to the point of what happened in Mostar on the 9th of May in the area where you lived. I mean, 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: On 9th of May, early in the morning, I was awakened by shooting, intense shooting, which could be heard in the city. I turned on the radio, and on the radio, people of Bosniak ethnicity were called to put out a white cloth in the sign of surrender and nothing would happen to them. And there were also Croat nationalist songs being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: On behalf of whom was that statement made? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: On behalf of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened to you and to your family on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: During the morning, three HVO soldiers entered the apartment where I was living. They searched the apartment, and they ordered me to come out in front of the building. There were some other persons there alongside with me, and then they took us to the Velez stadium in a van. In the stadium itself there were a lot of people, including women and children. And several hours later, they took us from the stadium to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just -- I would like to clarify one question: Before you were taken from your apartment, did they take over your keys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they explain to you why you were supposed to leave your flat, your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: They were armed. They had automatic rifles, and that was a very strong argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you a civilian at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Maybe for some minutes, Your Honour, we could go now into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know any other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we're in the open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, what did you observe at the stadium area? What categories of people were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: There were several categories of people there, including the elderly, including the women, including even small children, infants, there were even some of those. In other words, all categories were included.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many people, in your estimate, were taken from the stadium to Heliodrom? If you can, you can. Just an approximate figure, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say, but at the Heliodrom, there were certainly several thousand people who were brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were all the buildings of Heliodrom occupied by prisoners on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Several buildings. I wouldn't be able to say whether all the buildings were occupied by them, but several buildings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: In which building were you kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I was in the building which they referred to as the central building, and I was on the first floor. In fact, it's not the first floor. It is the ground floor where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, the Trial Chamber has already been informed that on the 13th of May, Heliodrom prisoners were registered by the Red Cross, and on the 19th of May, after General Morillon visited Heliodrom, most of the prisoners were released. So I will not ask you questions on this issue. I just would like to know if you were released along with other prisoners on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No, I was not released on the 19th of May. Simply put, release took a while, and General Morillon left, and I was not released with a number of other prisoners. And our names were read out, we were separated out, and we were taken back to one of these rooms in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many prisoners were not released from Heliodrom on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: 102 prisoners were not released. I know the exact numbers because we had to all sign, and I know that we were separated into two groups of 51 each, so that a total of 102 prisoners that I know of were not released.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they explain to you why - I mean not you personally but other prisoners as well - why they did not release you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No. Of course, they did not give any explanations to anyone. However, I believe - and later on it turned out - that we were all of an age which made us able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Where did they take you from Heliodrom to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: From the Heliodrom, my group was taken to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many people, prisoners, were taken from Heliodrom to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Fifty-one prisoners were taken from the Heliodrom to Ljubuski, but there were other prisoners in Ljubuski who had been there from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask you to go into private session for some minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, as it follows from your prior witness statements, at some point in mid-June, you were returned to Heliodrom, stayed there for a certain period of time, and then you were transferred to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber about this period of time. First of all, how many prisoners were taken there from Heliodrom, and how long did they keep them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: First the group of 51 of us went from Ljubuski. And that is not only them but some others who were in Ljubuski on the 1st July. As far as I know, all these prisoners were transferred to the Heliodrom from Dretelj. One day before that, there were combat operations going on throughout Mostar, at the northern camp and the Bijelo Polje bowl which the ABiH liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you briefly inform the Trial Chamber about the conditions of detention of prisoners in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: In Dretelj, the conditions were very tough. I know that for a period of time - I think around the 13th of July - they kept us without food for three days and for two days without water, and there were also frequent beatings of the prisoners. Certain HVO soldiers were coming to several structures where I was, and they beat prisoners. They beat on one occasion too. They were firing from machine-guns at the height of about 1 metre, and it was a tin -- corrugated metal wall, and some people were -- some people were wounded. I was also hit by a piece of debris and slightly grazed. So the conditions were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that about 18th, 20th of July you were taken back to Heliodrom and then for some period of time you were transferred to the area of Doljani and Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What was your task in Doljani and Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Our task was - in this area, that is - to assist in building fortifications, and also because there had been fighting there between the ABiH and the HVO. Before that, we assisted in recovering the HVO soldiers who were killed, and we also dug graves for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Is it correct that somewhere towards the end of August, you were taken from Heliodrom to Vojno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber what kind of detention unit Vojno was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Unlike the Heliodrom where the ICRC also came, this was a facility where the Red Cross did not come, that is, they did not have access there. In this camp, people who were kept included the civilians, women and children, and the conditions were very difficult. They were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who was in charge of Vojno detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: The person in charge, obviously it was under the HVO control, I think it was -- that the 2nd Brigade was in charge, and Mario Mihalj was the commander of this camp. And what I would also like to point out in that regard was that there were also members of the Croatian army present there, and that's when I -- where I saw them for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that they were from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I know because they had the HV insignia. "HV" stands for the Croatian army. And also, we were on one occasion lined up by a man who was probably some officer of the Croatian army. And the reason why I'm saying this was that he criticised the HVO. He said, "You from the HVO only shoot. You are wasting ammunition," while the other side was not doing this. And his accent was not from this area. I believe he could have come from Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did they retain you to Heliodrom after Vojno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I stayed there some two weeks at Vojno, and I was returned, I think, sometime in the early days of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever perform any labour in Mostar? I mean the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, several times, but most of the time I spent working at Stela's.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You just named a person named Stela. Had you known him before you were taken to work for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, yes, because in the beginning of the war, that is, in 1992, he was a HOS commander, H-O-S commander, so that I saw him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Vinko Martinovic, called Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of position he occupied in 1993 when you were taken to Mostar to work for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: He commanded Vinko Skrobo unit, and he was usually called either "Colonel" or "General." Men used to use both these ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Vinko Skrobo, do you know what stands for this name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I don't. It's a Croat name, so he's a Croat, but I don't know who or what he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Don't you remember any famous Croats from, let's say, the former Yugoslavia history?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is rather leading. The witness said he didn't know, so why lead him in this manner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it is a leading question. You may skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of unit was it, Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, that was an ATG unit, and it made part of the Convicts Battalion from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Part of the Convicts Battalion. Do you know who Stela's commander was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Why, that was Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Once - I think it was in November - Mr. Martinovic went to attend a meeting at Tuta's, and on that occasion, somebody fired at him. That is, on his way, he was fired at. And soldiers from that unit talked about that, and that is how I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did Stela's soldiers have? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: There were different uniforms. There was the conventional camouflage uniform, then also green -- I mean completely green, rather light-green uniform, and some also had black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You just told the Trial Chamber that soldiers used to address Stela as "Colonel" or "General." Did he have the insignia of a colonel or a general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No, he didn't, or at least, I never saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were taken first to perform job for that unit? I mean Vinko Skrobo unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. We were brought to the garage; that is where we were put up. In the morning, we were assigned tasks, and I and several other persons were taken to the front line, to the -- where they held their positions. That was next to the Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Let's talk about the garage first. Where was that garage located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: It was on Kalemova Street. And these are buildings across the street from the command of the Vinko Skrobo unit. The first -- no, the second building, across the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Have you ever been inside of that building? I mean the building that was used for the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. Once, if I remember well, I went there. They held a small area where they stored weapons, and I think I had to get something there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did you see that building last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: It could have been about 15 days ago, except that it looks completely different now. I mean, it's been renovated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: If I show you a picture of the building, perhaps you could identify it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Perhaps. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like usher -- our witness to be shown Exhibit number 15.2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: This building has three large letters, "HVO." So there are these three letters, "HVO," and I did -- I did see it quite recently, and there is always somebody there, and it is this HVO building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But is it the same building that was used as headquarters by Vinko Skrobo's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: This building was redone, rebuilt completely. But that's where, beforehand, was the building which housed the Vinko Skrobo command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: For example, could you tell me what has changed in the building, in the shape of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, it would be easier to say what hasn't changed, because practically everything is changed. The facade is different. The entrance was not from this side. It looks completely different now. The entrance was on the other side, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You may take it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, how long did they keep you in garage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I was there between the 21st of September, 1993 until early December that year. All the time I spent at Stela's, and all the time, except for the first ten days, I spent in the garage. The first ten days or a fortnight, I was at the front line -- I mean in a -- in the Health Centre building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Let's move to the Health Centre building now. Do you remember that area now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did you see it last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I went there every day. I passed through that area every day twice, twice every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Has it changed much since 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, that area was renovated. Three buildings are as they were, except that they were done up and slightly changed. There is a new building, and a part of the old building was demolished, but you could say that practically all the buildings are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see Stela on the confrontation line area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, yes, a number of times. I saw him in that area and also at the headquarters at the main command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did he give you any orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Now and then. Now and then he would be the one who would assign people to places, saying, "You're going there. You are going here," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, usher, I would like you to show the Witness YY Exhibit number 14.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the area depicted in the picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Would you inform the Trial Chamber which buildings in that area were occupied or were used by Vinko Skrobo unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to point it with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: This building here, this one, this one, this one, and this one is -- looks now completely different than in 1993. So it is this area here. Those -- this was the area under Vinko Skrobo unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's begin with the first building indicated by you. Take a marker and just put number "1" on this building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What did they have in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: In this -- in that building, they had beds and a dormitory on the ground floor and a place where coffee was made. On the upper floor was a machine-gun nest; that is, it was a combat position. And between the two, in the mezzanine, was a room where we slept for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You said "dormitory." Do you mean dormitory for soldiers or for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Like this. In the basement, in the cellar, was the place where soldiers slept, those who were on -- who had been assigned to the front line and who -- therefore, some were at guard posts and others rested. As for me and other prisoners - and we were 14 - we were in the mezzanine, or rather, on the first floor, and there was a room where we slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go across the street now. The big building that was indicated by you, put number "2" on it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What was that building used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: In that building, there was another combat position. On the upper Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. floor, we had to make small openings which could be used by snipers. And we also removed the floor, the parquet, because it -- and it was used to heat the building, as fuel wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now go back to the medical centre itself. Put number "3" on it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know if that building was rebuilt, or does it keep its previous shape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was it rebuilt or keeps the previous shape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, more or less the same shape now. Whether every detail is there, whether every door is there, I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what did they have in that building, in building number 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: They had their bunkers and guard posts in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you make some job in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. In this area, we fortified -- I mean, we filled bags with sand or earth and carried them to fortify the positions held by the soldiers, and some other positions as well, which were not manned, and we would fortify those areas too with sandbags.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We have not finished with the buildings yet. You have indicated before one more building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Put a number "4" on it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And again, I would like you to explain for what purposes was that building used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: That building, this is a new building. The one that was there before was -- faced in a different direction, 90 degrees. So this is a new building. But in that earlier building, they also had a guard post. And between buildings 1 and the building that was in place of the building number 4, they also -- because this place was well-shielded, and they sometimes launched their rockets from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was Vinko Skrobo the only unit that was in charge of Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No. There were some other units too, but this one held this area which I've marked with numbers. Tuta north and Tuta south. But there were some other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know the names of those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And what kind of job did you perform on the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: As for these jobs, that is, jobs involving fortification, well, we filled those bags with sand, fortified those positions. And on the front line itself, in those early days, we made coffee for soldiers. And at the same time, we performed a number of jobs for soldiers in that unit, in flats around Mostar, that is, we were taking out furniture, household appliances, and other things of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to take away this exhibit for a moment, and we'll pass on to another one. My next exhibit will be P11.18.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: If I may add, I'd like to say something else that I did on this front line. It was sometime in late September. At that time, a rather large group of Bosniaks was expelled across this area, from the west into the east side, and since a large number -- a large quantity of clothing had remained behind them, the next day, a soldier, Solaja, ordered me to go through this large pile of clothes, or rather, check the hems of those clothes, I presume thinking that people had hidden money or perhaps some other valuables that they had sewn into those hems, so that I, and later on he joined me, and we went over all the hems and seams of those clothes, but we didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So we must return to our Exhibit 14.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like usher to place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you indicate on the map the route those civilians were moving across the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, I can, yes. So they would come from behind building 2 and take this route.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to take the marker and just to put some dotted line showing the way they were moving.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Just you should put an arrow in the end of their route indicating the direction they were moving.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was it the only occasion that you saw civilians crossing the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I can tell you about that period of time. There was an incident one night when one of the soldiers came and woke us up and we went to behind building number 2. There was a broken truck, a truck which wouldn't move, so we had to push it, and eventually it started off. And on that occasion, we saw a large number of people who were there. After that, we returned. And of course I couldn't fall asleep immediately after we returned and nor could all those others. So what we heard was how -- well, they usually shouted, "Balija, those, your men for you," and would let them go. And in the morning, one could see large number -- large quantities of clothes and bags and all sorts of things. And there was another incident, and that was again sometime around that time when in the afternoon -- one afternoon, and I was doing something - I don't know exactly what - and two elderly men and two women came, arrived. They checked their documents, and one of those men who was of quite -- he was elderly, but he was under 60. That is what the soldier said. So they let those other three go and took this one somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Let's return for the moment to the first -- to the first group of civilians that were crossing the confrontation line. What categories of civilians did you see among those people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Witness YY has spoken now of several incidents. I just would like to know for the record if we're speaking about the first incident in late September with the soldier by the name of Solaja. Is this the incident we're speaking of? If not, let us know which incident we're speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, would you please make it clear for us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would just like you to expand a little bit on the incident which you -- you just indicated the route of movement of the civilians from one side to the other side. Just my question was relevant to that incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me explain the first situation first. At night, this soldier from this unit came. We helped push the truck which he couldn't start. Then he started it and left. And behind building number 2 there was a large crowd. But after the truck had started, we were taken back, but we could still hear. This went on for several days. A large group of people was expelled. And then the next day, the soldier named Solaja demanded, ordered me to check all hems for valuables. So that was one situation. And another situation on another day, on another time, the situation was that the two elderly men and two also women who were advanced in age, and when these people were let through to the east side, one of the men was kept behind, kept back because he was not yet 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is clear about that second, let's say, incident. I'm asking you about the first incident. Who were among the civilians? That's what I would like to ask you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Among these civilians were elderly men, women, and children. There were -- the able-bodied men were not among them. That category was not there from what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Now you really can put aside this exhibit, and let's now return to the job that you mentioned some minutes before as taking valuables from flats, some flats in some parts of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who ordered you to do this job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: The soldiers who were members of that unit. They would come and select some of us and would take them to the apartments which they had pre-selected. Then they would order that the belongings which they would choose then be loaded onto these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember any names of Vinko Skrobo unit, I mean, soldiers who ordered you to do this job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I do. Ernest Takac, called Brada, was one of them; Zdena Ilicic; and there were some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just wait a moment because the transcript is lagging behind. I would like you to repeat the names because there is something wrong about the spelling of one of the names. So --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Ernest Takac, called Brada. And Zdena Ilicic, it is spelled Z-d-e-n-a, first name, I-l-i-c-i-c. And there was a Zdena whose last -- whose name I don't recall, and there were some others there whose names I cannot give you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you involved in this job frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, both myself and others worked there on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you have an idea to whom those apartments belonged before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you the names, but they were not among the soldiers who were taking these belongings. There were some other names there. They were not the owners. They were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But were those apartments abandoned by the time you were taking away belongings from them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. There were no owners in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And what kind of valuables did you take from the flats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: It was furniture, the refrigerators, washing machines, various kinds of stoves, paintings, television sets, video recorders, whatever was of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And where did they take those things after loading them on the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Those -- sometimes we would just load up the goods, and then they would leave. Sometimes they would go to the garages which they had, I guess some kind of storage places of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And now I would like you to take a look at the map of Mostar, and maybe you'll be able to show the Trial Chamber the places, the locations, where you participated in the looting of houses. Of course, I realise that most of the streets have changed their names, but which is better for you, to use traditional, prior names of the streets, or now, current names of the streets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: This is the area that used to be called Dum. This is Ante Zvanica, the Omladinska Street. In Centar II, I know that we also went there. So that is about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you just to take a marker and encircle those areas and put some numbers in them. And of course, with your comments, how was or is this -- the name of this street or area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: So there was the neighbourhood of Dum. Let me just find it near Liska. That is Dum. And also several buildings on Liska Street, Liska. Ante Zvanica, Omladinska Street, and Centar II. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to put numbers on each circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: So this is the Dum area; Liska Street; Ante Zvanica, number 3; Omladinska, number 4; and Centar II, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You may put it aside now. Witness, how did Stela's soldiers treat prisoners while you were performing some job in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: We had to work on these jobs. They ordered us what to do. Some of the prisoners occasionally would be getting hit. I did not. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember any names of soldiers who were mistreating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Ernest Takac was one of the worst ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But could you explain a little bit why did you come to such a conclusion that he was one of the worst?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Because on a number of occasions, he beat the prisoners and then also abused them verbally, and he also was the one who took the most effects from other apartments. I do not want to mention the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit number 704, just -- the original version is under ERN 00795386, the English version on page 30. Could you place it on the ELMO? I would like to check if we are on the same page. Mr. Usher, could you help him to put it on the ELMO, because I would like to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, have you leafed down this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see any names that were -- ring familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I do. They are Vinko Martinovic; Dubravko Pehar. Colak -- there were two, one was Mladen and there was another Colak. Then Ernest Takac. Solaja is also here. There was another Bosniak. There is Semir Bosnjic. There were some Germans there, but of course I did not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Witness, you informed the Trial Chamber that you were performing some sort of job on the confrontation line itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was there shooting or firing while you were performing your job on the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course there was shooting, because that was the front line. But during that period, that is, while I was there, that segment of the confrontation line, there were no offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When were you taken back to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: In early December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you perform any kind of job for other military units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I did. When we were brought back, we were going out to work less. But on one occasion -- on one occasion, there were two units who were part of the Croatian army. They were the Tigers and the Thunderbolts. They were their guard units. On one occasion, the members of the Tigers came and selected several of us from among the prisoners, and we were taken in the direction of Buna where they had a forward position. On our way there, we were mistreated. They would stop the vehicle, and they would beat us. When we arrived at the bridge on Buna - this is, the new bridge built over the Buna river in 1993 - they brought the vehicle to a stop, they ordered us out of the vehicle, and they ordered us to crawl across the bridge. They said that they would slit our throats, that they would kill us, that they would throw us into the Neretva River. They beat us. Then they again ordered us to board the vehicle, the truck, and we came to a facility at Buna where they again mistreated us for several hours, threatened us and occasionally beat. Then they stopped doing that, and close to the evening, they brought us back to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And how did you learn the names of the unit that you mentioned, Tigrovi and Thunderbolts? Tigers, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: We learned of those names because certain prisoners were going over there every day and helped them with preparing food, with cleaning up and whatever they needed, and they were going every day. And they had insignia, and you could read the name of their unit, the Tigers, and also the HV sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When were you released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I was released in March when this big exchange or release took place after the Washington Accords were signed between the Bosniaks and Croats, that is, when based on that agreement, the Heliodrom camp was dissolved. And I believe that that was the 19th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: This was my final question. My examination-in-chief is over. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination? Mr. Par, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Perhaps we can take a break early, if you don't mind, or I could even start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we'll have a break right now, but we have to start ten minutes earlier. Usher, would you please take the witness out of the room first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll resume at twenty minutes past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, cross-examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I am Zelimir Par. I'm one of the Defence attorneys for Mr. Vinko Martinovic, and I'm going to ask you some questions in relation to the evidence you've given. First off, let me take you back to the building of the base. You saw a picture of it, and you described it, but I would like some further clarifications. My question is: Is this a completely new building that, by its look, does not resemble the old base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether this is a completely new building or it was completely reconstructed? I wouldn't be able to say that, but it is completely different from the building that I remember, at least from the outside; I don't know from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you: If somebody were to see this picture, they would not be able to see, based on the picture alone, that this was that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No. They would have to be there on location.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher now to please bring back the map which the Prosecutor had used, that is, 14.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And I would like the copy that you had marked. It has to do with the zone of responsibility of this unit, so I'm going to ask you some questions about that. Let's start with the -- where the people who were expelled at night were going. Is that behind building 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. It is between the building marked with "2" and the building that was not rebuilt and down the road and that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The question that I have is: Why did they not take that road straight down? Were there any obstacles there? Were there any sandbags there? Is that the reason why they did not take that street straight down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, you yourself have just given the answer. There were sandbags around here, and they were about 2 metres high in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would -- I need to ask the -- my learned friend whether they would object to my asking the witness to mark that same copy, or shall I give him a fresh copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: In principle, I don't object, but I'm concerned if they will not spoil my picture by their marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I believe that the marks will be on a different location; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'll provide a new map. But I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. will ask the witness to also make all the marks which he has done previously and then add something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So, Witness, let me ask you to just copy all the marks that you had made previously, and then we'll make some new ones.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And could you place the new one on the ELMO, and we can give back the old one used by the Prosecutor so we don't confuse it. Very well. So we have sandbags. Will you mark where the sandbags were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: It was on the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, where you showed them. I believe that it was between markers 1 and 2. And just the next number. That's 5, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very good. So as far as you can remember, it was sandbags here. And how high was this barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Over two metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, between 2 and 1, do you remember if there was a cord, a kind of a clothesline which -- over which some blankets or some canvas or something was hung to protect against sniper fire, rather, to screen people from sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I don't remember. Possibly there was something like that, but I just don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's now look at building number 3, which is the Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please do make a pause between questions and answers, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The Health Centre, building number 3, do you remember how many entrances were there into the Health Centre, and especially on the front side, just opposite the fountain? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: What you're asking me is whether there was an entrance door near the fountain, next to the fountain? Well, before the war, that is, in 1992, there was an entrance, and I think that was the dentist, where the dentist surgery was. But in 1993, of course the entrance could not be there because it -- it would have to face the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Was there a door there, whether one could go in and out, not whether people did go in and out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, before the war, before 1992, was the dentistry, was the dentist surgery where teeth were extracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But at that time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I didn't come out there, so I couldn't tell you. That is, nobody used that door to come out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You mean you were never in front of that building at that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No. I'll show you exactly. So right in front of this place, I put a point there. I was not there. Yes, before 1992, not after 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. While we still have this photograph in front of you and with this arrow, and we see where those expelled people moved, let us go back to that period of time and tell me if some Muslims or the majority of Muslims who stayed behind on the west bank, did they want to leave West Mostar of their own free will and cross over to the east side? Was that how the situation was or do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I was in the camp, and I wouldn't really be able to answer you that. Perhaps some other witnesses will be able to tell you more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And whilst you were there, whilst you were with this unit, did you perhaps witness some incidents when a Muslim from West Mostar came to that unit and said, "Will you please help me cross this line? Could you please provide safe passage for me?" Did it ever happen, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, on those two incidents that happened, I already described it as I saw them, and I did that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. But my question was if you saw there some people who wanted to cross of their own free will, whether some people volunteered to do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No, I did not. As far as I can remember, I did not see anyone come to any soldier and ask him to help him cross the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did I understand you well when you said when these people were crossing over that they noted -- that there was a notice that civilians were moving, therefore, not to open fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. I can repeat that. "Balijas, balijas. There, your people are coming." So they would go there, and they shouted that, and that happened on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, we know that you are eager to help us by giving your evidence, but whatever you say is to be translated into the other two languages. The interpreters are having a very difficult time to follow you both. So do please wait until you hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Mr. President. I will do my best to help the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Par, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, I will give you a sign when you need to make a short break, and if I'm too fast, then you warn me, please, and I hope we'll solve the problem. Now, let's touch upon your stay with the unit, the conditions under which you were kept there. You said that you first slept in a garage, then at some other place in one of those buildings there. Tell me, were you guarded on such occasions when you slept there? Were you under lock? What kind of supervision was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, whilst we were in the garage, they would lock the garage. I don't know who was outside. I suppose somebody was outside, but I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly. So they would take us in when the night falls and lock us up. As for this other part, that is, when we were on the front line, they would take us into the room. So there was nobody in front of the room exactly, but there were other armed men from the unit so that, of course, it never occurred to us to leave the room until somebody was called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I, rather, wanted to see if you felt there as a prisoner was there always somebody all over you or could you -- did you have any freedom of movement or something? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Listen --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. You can proceed now

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, you are free if you can go somewhere. Had I been free, I wouldn't have stayed there those three months. I would have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Well, no. I do -- I wasn't trying to prove that you were free. I wanted to compare it to other places that you've been to, and I wanted to ask you to tell us what kind of food was there. How about water? Could you compare the conditions at this place with the conditions at other places where you were kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, listen, food was short all the time. We never had any sufficient food anywhere. Now, to try to make some comparisons, well, it's difficult, but now when I look back at it, I think that Vojno was the worst of them all. Others, I don't think they would be -- they would easily -- they could be easily compared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But you say, "In one place we were 50 in one room so there was no room for us to lie down." Then could you sleep -- did you have more room to sleep over here? Was the food over there better? Was it better with this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I tried --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, do go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I tried to tell you that insofar as overall conditions were concerned, then I would say that Vojno was the worst. But now if I single out individual elements from here or -- and from there, it is difficult for me to say that. I think that it will be enough if I say that Vojno was the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Right. So Vojno was the worst, but Vojno is at Bijelo Polje, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, it is at Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question -- my other question is: Did Stela provide the best conditions of all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I couldn't say that Stela provided the best conditions because there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's move on to the unit. You said you knew quite a great deal about the unit, what kind of unit it is, who is a general, who is a colonel, what its name is. So let's touch upon that now. How many men were there in this unit, according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know. Thirty? Fifty? I don't really know. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. But roughly, would you say that that is the number of people that you saw around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts, yes, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You are saying that this unit's commander was Vinko Martinovic and that he was addressed as "Colonel" or "General"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, that's how they addressed him, or "Commander" perhaps. But I know, they would say "Colonel" or "General."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were there any other forms of address, whether they called him as "Chief" or "Stela"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I couldn't really remember now. I don't know. Possibly, but I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, you said, if I understood you properly, that you never saw him wear any rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I can't remember if he had anything. He was often in a greenish uniform, so that is one colour, but that was a greenish colour. But I cannot remember whether the HVO at that time even had any of these insignias, I mean to indicate a general or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, let's clear up this matter of address. When a soldier says "Colonel" or "General," when a soldier says that to his superior, is it, as in a regular army, when you have a soldier address his superior that way, or is it more in a kind of a conversation, a friendly way, in which somebody says "Colonel," "General" or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, what I have in mind is -- all I can say - and that is only my opinion - is that I do not think that he was officially a general or a colonel, but that is only my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, because you can't -- we can agree you can't address somebody now as a general and now as a colonel, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I think my learned friend is making statements instead of asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that question is answered in a perfect way. You may proceed, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness YY, did you serve the army? Did you serve the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you know that kind of organisation, this conventional military structure, as it should be, for instance, the one of the -- in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, yes, even though I'm no expert. I don't really know much about matters military, but I did serve in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to ask you anything special, just what an ordinary foot soldier would know. What I'm interested in is the organisation of this unit, the chain of command, the organisational layout, the relations between soldiers and their superiors. Could you draw a comparison between them and an army? So my question is, directly: Could you feel in that unit that you were in, could you really know who was -- who and who was what discipline, the chain of command? Was it a thing which was -- which was obvious? Was it evident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're asking me, but I did not see anyone reporting to anyone. But Mr. Martinovic clearly had that -- the command, so that their conversations, their talks, their reports, I suppose, took place inside the building. I wouldn't know, really. I don't know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I am particularly interested in. I'm interested in their organisation, because I want to find out whether that unit -- whether that unit's commander is completely in the know, everything that goes on. Is he kept abreast where is every one of the officers under him or soldiers, where his men are, what they are doing? Is there a proper organisation, as in every other army? Is there a clear picture, clear organisational layout?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, listen, I cannot answer that question, of course, because I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't really know what the relationships were between Mr. Stela and his men, the men who were under him. I cannot answer that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. You've already answered it. If I understood you properly, you were not able to see that, you were not able to observe the kind of the hierarchical ladder.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, what I could see was what they said, that Stela was the commander of that unit. Now, what their relations were, did he know what each one of his men did, that I really don't know because I wasn't a soldier in his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let us go back to that "Colonel," "General," the form of address. You mentioned that you knew that Stela had been with HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did they also address him as "General," "Colonel" then, when in HOS? What was he in HOS? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: He was a commander of a unit then, and they were cornered -- and they were then on the corner between the old and the new hospital in Mostar, and he was -- he commanded that unit. I remember that in 1992, there was -- there were some horses -- there was an open area, and there were some horses in front of that building, and he commanded that unit, but I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did HOS play a positive role in that time when it was defending Mostar against the Serb aggression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Would you say that it is possible that this address, this rank, "Colonel," "General," was attached to Stela at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, you are asking me something that I do not know, so it's better for me not to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I mean, did you hear anyone ask -- address him as "Colonel," "General," at that time, during the HOS period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I saw him only once at that time. I was nowhere near HOS at that time, and I wouldn't -- I couldn't really -- I wasn't in a position to know such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to show the witness now a document which has to do with this issue, and I'd like the witness to look at it, the ID D2/23. And the registrar has the copies for the Chamber, and I'd like also one copy to be given -- that the witness be given one of the copies. We gave the copies of this document to the Prosecutor during the break. Unfortunately, we do not have it in French for Judge Diarra because we did not expect that we would have to produce this document today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, could you please have a look at this document. Do you know what it is, what is the date on that document, and what rank is indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, it says here that this is the army membership card.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And which name is indicated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, beneath, it says "rank"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, the rank. It says "soldier."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can we look at the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. It says "19th of June, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. I'm showing you this document because I set out to prove that the term that you mentioned, that is, "General," "Colonel," is due -- arises from something else and not from his formal rank. Now, when you see this document, it shows that he did not have this official rank, even though somebody maybe addressed him with the rank.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I can repeat what I have already said. My opinion, that is, is that he did not have the official rank of a colonel or general, and I've already said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are coming to the end. I have only a few questions more, which have to do with those items taken from abandoned houses, in which you participated directly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So my question is: Was Stela ever present when you did those things, when you took those things out of houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: My answer is very short. No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: At what time of the day or night did this happen when you had to go with those people that you went with to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, it was either in daytime or at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know if anyone notified Stela about this, that this was going on and what was going on? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: A moment ago, I've already told you that being a prisoner, of course, I could not be in the possession of such information, what kind of relationships existed between Stela and other soldiers in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And we've just managed to establish a good pace between question and answer, and I've run out of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness YY. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Meek, and I'm one of the Defence counsel for Mladen Naletilic, and I have a few questions for you this morning. First, do you understand that you were a member of the army of JNA in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of the military, either prior to the incidents in 1993 or subsequent to your release from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Well, I, some ten years before the conflict in BH, I did my military service with the JNA, like all the able-bodied men in the then-Yugoslavia, and I was also a member of the reserve police force and attended sometime in September 1992 of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: After your release from the Heliodrom, you never went back to the military, and you were never an active member of any military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, if you ask some questions which touch upon the protective measures, just inform the Court. We could easily go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. I didn't believe I did, but I will certainly bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then, may we go into private session for a moment, just to be sure, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness YY, I noticed that you gave two separate statements, one in January, on the 27th, of 1996, in Mostar to the criminal police sector; and then a second statement you gave the 1st of October, 1998 to members of the office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal. Are these the only two statements you've given concerning your -- the events of your life in 1993 until your release in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: No. I have given another statement. In fact, there was a short statement given at the Heliodrom; this is to some HVO policemen. They asked some questions very briefly. And I also gave a statement in 1994, after we were released from the camp. And that was also a statement given to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you say "the police," was that the AID or the secret police in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: It was the police, the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness YY, would it be a fair conclusion that you reviewed the statement of January 27, 1996 and also reviewed your October 1, 1998 statement prior to coming to the Tribunal to testify? And if you don't understand, I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Could you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you have a chance, the opportunity to read the statements that you gave in 1996 and again in 1998, which bear your signature, before you came to The Hague to testify today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Before today, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that today you testified in your direct examination that this Stela person had an ATG unit and that you testified today that it made a part of the Convicts Battalion out of Siroki Brijeg? You testified to that today. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, I said that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Witness YY, that when you gave your statements in 1996, in January 1996, the events which had occurred in your life in 1993 and early 1994 were fresher on your mind than they are today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: They probably were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the same answer would probably apply, would it not, to the statement you gave to the OTP in October of 1998, three years ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that you never mentioned in either one of these statements that the -- you never mentioned Convicts Battalion nor did you ever mention Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: As far as these statements are concerned, as far as I recall, they were not mentioned. But even today in this hearing, I did not mention everything that concerns these statements. In other words, I just answered the questions asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it's my understanding from your testimony today that you believed, or it's your opinion that this individual named Tuta was somehow in charge of this ATG unit in Mostar, based simply on the fact that you had heard talk about Stela going to this town of Siroki Brijeg to have a meeting and somebody shot at his car.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: On one occasion, Stela went to that meeting, and somebody shot at his vehicle. And this is why the soldiers talked about it more than usual, because it is something that held their interest more. So from what they were saying, one could infer that Tuta was some kind of their chief, somebody who was superior to them, somebody above Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again Witness YY, that's an inference you drew from comments made by other people or third parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness YY, I wish you the best of luck in life, and thank you for coming all this way to testify to this Honourable Tribunal. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a very short one. I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit number 704. It is page 30 of the English Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. version and B/C/S version ERN 00795386, just the same document I showed to the witness sometime before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you, Witness, just to look at the right side of the list. Do you see Vinko Martinovic's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of position did he have according to this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: On the basis of this list, here it is stated that he had a commanding position, in other words, that he was a commander of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. And the second person, the person who is under number 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Dubravko Pehar, deputy commander. In other words, he is a deputy of the commander of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Number 5?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Five, Ernest Takac, group leader. That means that he led one of these groups, one of these shifts, one of these teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my objection goes to the form of these questions. This document speaks for itself. Why are we having this witness read number 1, number 4, number 5, and then go to the right? We can all read English or French. I object. It's not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. Show us your purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually I have received the response of my witness to the question that I had, and my intention was just to confront this document with a document showed by my learned colleague during the cross; I mean, the identification card, where Vinko Martinovic was mentioned just as a private. That's the only reason that I had for my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that document is still on the ELMO, I have a few questions for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no. Not now. There should be an end for the cross-examination, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This document was shown on the ELMO during direct examination. If you have any questions, you may raise it in your cross-examination, but not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not after the redirect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There were issues that came up on the redirect that I wish to question him about very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm in your hands, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, do you have the original of that document that you handed in to the witness, the identification of Vinko Martinovic? I'll tell you why I ask. The photograph is so poor that I thought you were putting it to the witness in order to establish that there was somebody else called Vinko Martinovic in the unit, because I have to say the photograph doesn't look at all like your client. But then nine years does change --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief. There is the original extant. I don't have it here. It is -- it may be at the detention unit, or we may have it. But there is -- the original does exist, to ask -- to answer the first question. And as far as the picture is concerned, the picture that is on that military ID was the exact same one that was provided to us from the OTP in one of the binders, blown up, the same exact picture of our client, Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness YY, can I ask you a question? When you were a member of the JNA, I understand - and correct me if I'm wrong about this - that all men of military age had to do some sort of very minimal training in the JNA, for some period of 12 to 14 months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Twelve to eighteen months is what the training took, and it wasn't really minimal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
