utterances.text: So when you were there, would you have had to take orders from a corporal and then a sergeant and work your way up through the non-commissioned officers and recognise the titles and ranks of the officer brigade or unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Yes. A corporal, and so on and so forth, had his own rank and then commanded accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I was just wondering: Had you ever come across the title "Commander"? It's not one that translates in English as something that one finds in the army, "Commander," in English anyway. It's something that you may have, maybe, in the naval service, but in the army, were you familiar with the title "Commander"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Commanding officer or commander, I'm afraid I didn't quite understand. It is the person who commands, the person who is in charge of a unit. This is what he is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The reason I ask that is that in army titles that are known to me, you start with the lieutenant and then a captain, and then a major and a colonel and different types of generals from a major general a brigadier general and a full general, but I don't know the title "Commander." Do you know of a title that an officer carries called "Commander"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: Now I fully understand your question. The commander, as I was using it, it is not a rank, it is not like a lieutenant. It is somebody that command a unit, regardless of whether the unit is one commanded by a lieutenant, a major, a captain. But it is a person who commands a unit. It is not a particular rank that one has on his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness YY, on that Exhibit 704 that had "Commander" and other list --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. What's the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Because Judge Clark didn't touch upon this question during her examination relevant to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but Judge Clark asked the question about "Commander." I think the Defence counsel has the right to ask questions concerning with this title, if I may say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I tried to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness YY, Judge Clark had asked you questions about the names on this list, this 704 document, that was close there to you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think I did. I just asked about the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe I went overboard there a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But very briefly, you don't know who drew that document up, do you? You don't know who drew that document up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: What I -- I can read what is written there, but I don't know more -- anything more about that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS YY
utterances.text: That is -- what I could read was, as far as I can recall -- is the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: During this time that you were in Mostar, that you talked about, you never ever saw Mr. Naletilic, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this is not a question that is stemming from Judge Clark's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, this question is out of the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He was just ready to answer no, Your Honour. We have 45 minutes, and we are done. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. There should be a rule, no matter how much time we have left. There must be a rule in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, then, Merry Christmas to everybody, a good life to you, and I thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. We all wish you Merry Christmas and Happy New Year.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NALETILIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please be silent. The usher will show you out of the room when he pulls down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to tender the following documents: Exhibits P11.18/9, P14.5/10, P15.2. The documents P704 and 745.1 have already been tendered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, the witness is gone. Your Honour, Mr. President, we have no objection to P11.18/9, P14.5/10, P15.2. We have filed our written objection to P745.1 this morning, which was brought forward last week through a witness. The same objections would apply to this witness. We have previously objected to P704 on the grounds as identically to P745.1, so those objections are already on the record. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Those documents that were not objected to by Defence counsel are admitted into the evidence. Are there any documents to tender from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are the documents: D2/23, which is the military ID, and D2/24, which is the map that -- that is the photograph that the witness has marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, I would like to have a look at the original document first, because it's very difficult to see something from the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It cannot be, let's say, legible, and the image of the person in the picture is not quite clear, if it is the same Vinko Martinovic, because we know that "Martinovic" name was very common in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and apparently "Vinko" is also a very well-known name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I suggest that you allow us to produce this document when we're able to also produce the original, and at that time we will also present the photograph that we were provided by the OTP. So I would like to reserve right, after we come back from the recess, to come back to the admission, the admissibility of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: There was a mistake. The Exhibit 14.5/11 it should be, not 10. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So the document D2/24, which originally was P14.5, marked by the witness, is admitted into the evidence. Thank you. Well, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Two points before the very end, because we're about to go into the recess. I would like to ask, Mr. President, through you, to request our learned friends to give us the witness list so that we start our preparations for what is ahead of us after the 7th of January. And then on behalf of both teams, I would like to wish Merry Christmas and happy holidays to everybody concerned and also happy birthdays to all those who happen to have them between now and the 7th of January, when we next see you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is there any response from the Prosecution side about the list of the witnesses for the next year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That will be provided in short order. As you know, Mr. President, Your Honours, we've done that all along, and we'll continue to follow our practice of doing that. I would expect that can be -- the witnesses for January, that can be done in reasonably short order and provided, and there's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. And could you inform us how many witnesses, potential witnesses, are you planning to call upon after the New Year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that question is a bit difficult to answer because there are a number of requests for certain orders outstanding, and it depends upon -- depends on the witnesses who ultimately agree or come to The Hague. So it's difficult for me to answer that question because it could range considerably, depending on the witnesses who agreed to appear. I would suspect that we're looking somewhere in the vicinity - and forgive the wide range, Your Honour, but it's the most honest answer I can give you - would be somewhere depending between -- anywhere between 10 and 20 witnesses approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how long are you going to take for your direct examination after the Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, our estimate is based upon -- our understanding is that we will commence proceedings again on approximately Monday, the 7th of January. I would hope to be able to conclude the Prosecution case in not more than, and hopefully with some good fortune, perhaps less, but approximately three weeks, starting on the 7th of January. So that would take us, if all -- if, and again I have to -- I'm sorry I have to qualify my answers so much. But depending on the witnesses who appear, if they all will appear, then I suppose it should take us until the latter part of January, but no later than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. At this stage, are there any matters to bring to the attention of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just have two, Your Honour, briefly. One is just before we recess, I have a bundle of translations here that have come in concerning documents that were used with Mr. Prelec the first time he appeared, and those translations became available to me this morning. And just as a matter of record, I'll make them available to counsel and to your staff in the course of the day. I have them here. And secondly, Your Honour, I will certainly join in with the Defence and certainly on behalf of the entire Prosecution team to wish the -- all of you and your staffs and the Translation Unit our best wishes for the holiday recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we are adjourned until the 7th of January next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of January, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
